scopeNote: These are narrow, source-traceable comparisons of selected commitments. They do not classify a respondent or reconstruct a whole philosopher or tradition.

profiles.label: Philosophical anarchism — general content-independent obedience criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: One comparison criterion: whether there is a general moral duty to obey law merely because it is law. This does not reconstruct philosophical anarchism as a whole.
neighbors: Prudential or moral reasons to comply without a general duty
nonEntailments: Immediate abolition of the state
Rejection of voting, courts, or all institutions
Violence, resistance, or refusal to comply in every case
The claim that no law can create any moral reason for action
Moral skepticism
unmeasuredAreas: The full range of arguments for and against political obligation
Institutional alternatives, transition, and the practical feasibility of anarchist arrangements
Whether democracy, consent, fairness, or consequences can ground particular obligations

claims.targetText: The philosophical-anarchist position about a general content-independent duty to obey, not a policy of immediate institutional abolition.

sourceClaims.locator: Chapter I, section 3, conclusion on autonomy and a duty to obey laws simply because they are laws.
sourceClaims.claim: Wolff's argument denies that citizens have a general duty to obey state laws solely because they are laws; this is one argument within philosophical anarchism.
The scholarly overview treats philosophical-anarchist arguments as challenges to a general obligation to obey law and distinguishes variants of those arguments.

nonEntailments: State abolition
A specific institutional replacement
Violent methods
No reason to comply with any law
limitations: The active WVS target is a narrowly scoped comparison rule; it does not settle competing arguments or internal variants.
PLI048 and the other mapped items concern the stated obligation criterion, not every reason for compliance.
This is a single-criterion comparison, not a complete philosophical-anarchist profile.
Do not infer abolition, institutional rejection, tactics, or general noncompliance from this result.

profiles.label: Pragmatism — pragmatic-maxim criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: The pragmatic maxim as a method for clarifying concepts and apparent disputes through conceivable practical or experiential bearings; not a complete account of pragmatism.
neighbors: Consequences as one useful clarification technique
nonEntailments: A belief is true merely because it is useful
A complete pragmatist theory of truth
Rejection of mind-independent reality
Reduction of all meaningful claims to observation
A political or religious position
unmeasuredAreas: Pragmatist theories of truth and realism
The roles of inquiry, community, habit, and experimental practice across pragmatist traditions
Differences among Peirce, James, Dewey, and later pragmatists

claims.targetText: Disputed ideas should be clarified through their conceivable effects on experience or conduct; if two formulations have no conceivable difference in those effects, their apparent conceptual difference is not substantive.

sourceClaims.locator: Part II, Peirce's statement and explanation of the pragmatic maxim.
sourceClaims.claim: Peirce's maxim clarifies a conception by considering the conceivable practical bearings of its object.

sourceClaims.locator: Sections 2 and 2.1; compare sections 3.1 and 3.2 for variation about truth.
sourceClaims.claim: The scholarly account presents Peirce's maxim as a method for clarifying hypotheses through experience while documenting disagreement among pragmatists about truth and reality.

nonEntailments: Truth is whatever works
Antirealism
Scientific method as a complete philosophy
limitations: Only the stated clarification criterion is represented; the full tradition is not.
The active item set does not distinguish all pragmatist accounts of truth, realism, or inquiry.
The profile does not claim to measure every pragmatist doctrine or settle internal disagreement.
The direct criterion is available only on the Full route; its omission on Quick or Standard is not opposition.

profiles.label: Charles S. Peirce — pragmatic clarification and fallibilist inquiry (scoped)
profiles.scope: Two selected commitments in Peirce's work: pragmatic clarification and the fallibility of knowledge claims. This is not a whole-philosopher reconstruction.
neighbors: Pragmatism with different views of truth or realism
nonEntailments: Peirce's complete theory of truth or reality
Skepticism or epistemic pessimism
The doctrines of tychism, synechism, or agapism
Peirce's semiotics, categories, or complete theory of inquiry
unmeasuredAreas: Semiotics and the theory of signs
Categories, normative sciences, and the architectonic structure of his philosophy
Tychism, synechism, agapism, and the detailed account of truth and reality
Abduction and the full logic of scientific inquiry

claims.targetText: Disputed ideas should be clarified through their conceivable effects on experience or conduct; if two formulations have no conceivable difference in those effects, their apparent conceptual difference is not substantive.

sourceClaims.locator: Part II, 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear.'
sourceClaims.claim: Peirce formulates the pragmatic maxim as clarifying a conception through the conceivable practical bearings of its object.
The scholarly reconstruction identifies the maxim as central to Peirce's original conception of pragmatism.

nonEntailments: A full Peircean system
One theory of truth shared by all pragmatists
limitations: This question represents the maxim's selected clarification role, not Peirce's complete philosophical system.

claims.targetText: A claim can count as knowledge even when its justification leaves open a possibility of error.

sourceClaims.locator: Collected Papers 1.141–1.175, especially section 1.141 on the limits of certainty in reasoning.
sourceClaims.claim: Peirce argues that reasoning about factual matters cannot achieve absolute certainty; this claim is about fallibility, not that all beliefs are false.

sourceClaims.locator: Introduction and sections 2–3 on fallible justification and the possibility of knowledge.
sourceClaims.claim: The scholarly account distinguishes the possibility of error in justification from skepticism and explains how fallible justification can be compatible with knowledge.

sourceClaims.locator: Section 2, discussion of the fallibilist, anti-Cartesian norms of inquiry.
sourceClaims.claim: The scholarly account connects Peircean pragmatism with fallibilist inquiry while distinguishing Peirce's framework from other pragmatist views.

neighbors: Infallibilism about some kinds of knowledge
nonEntailments: No knowledge is possible
All beliefs are false
A particular respondent's confidence is low
limitations: The WVS proposition concerns the possibility of fallible knowledge, not the whole range or scope of Peirce's fallibilism.
The comparison does not test Peirce's arguments about science, continuity, or objective chance.
Two selected commitments cannot stand in for Peirce's broad and internally connected body of work.
The pragmatic-maxim criterion is Full-only; Quick and Standard results leave that central criterion unmeasured.

profiles.label: Empiricism about concrete external facts — experiential-warrant criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: One epistemic criterion: experiential evidence is ultimately required for knowledge claims about concrete external reality. It does not represent empiricism as a whole.
neighbors: Empiricism about the origin of concepts
Rationalist accounts of a priori external-world knowledge
nonEntailments: All knowledge comes from sensory experience
Reasoning is unimportant or dispensable
A denial of a priori knowledge in mathematics or ethics
Naive realism or a complete theory of perception
unmeasuredAreas: The source of concepts and the existence of innate ideas
Whether a priori knowledge is possible in mathematics, logic, ethics, or other domains
The structure of perception and the relation between experience and external objects

claims.targetText: Knowledge claims about concrete external reality ultimately require experiential evidence; reasoning alone cannot establish new external-world facts.

sourceClaims.locator: Sections 1.1–1.2, on empiricism and knowledge of the external world.
sourceClaims.claim: The scholarly account frames empiricism and rationalism partly in terms of whether experience is required for knowledge of external-world facts, while allowing reasoning to organize evidence.

sourceClaims.locator: Book IV, chapter XI, especially sections 1 and 3–6.
sourceClaims.claim: Locke distinguishes intuitive knowledge of one's existence, demonstrative knowledge of God, and sensitive knowledge of other things; this illustrates why the WVS comparison is restricted to external-world factual warrant.

nonEntailments: A complete Locke profile
Universal empiricism about every domain
Rejection of deduction or scientific reasoning
limitations: Only a subject-scoped external-world warrant criterion is represented.
The WVS target cannot distinguish all historical or contemporary forms of empiricism.
This criterion must not be presented as a complete empiricist worldview or as a classification of Locke.
The criterion is available only on the Full route; omission from shorter routes remains unmeasured.

profiles.label: Act consequentialism — direct maximizing rightness criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: One criterion: an act's own consequences directly determine its moral rightness, with a better available outcome ruling out a worse act. The profile does not identify utilitarianism or a theory of value.
nonEntailments: Utilitarianism
Welfarism
Hedonism
Impartial maximizing across all persons in every formulation
An empirically calibrated moral type
unmeasuredAreas: What counts as good or bad outcome value
Whether welfare is the only intrinsic good
The full scope of impartiality and aggregation
How the criterion applies to demandingness, rights, and side constraints

claims.targetText: An act’s own consequences ultimately determine its moral rightness, and an available act with a better outcome for everyone affected rules out a worse act as permissible.

sourceClaims.locator: Sections 1–2 and 5, distinguishing direct act criteria, maximization, rule criteria, and decision procedures.
sourceClaims.claim: The scholarly account defines act consequentialism by the consequences of the act and a maximizing rightness condition, while distinguishing it from rule consequentialism and from decision procedures.

nonEntailments: Utilitarianism
Welfarism
Hedonism
A single recommended decision procedure
limitations: The criterion does not state what makes outcomes good or bad.
The active route presents the direct criterion only in Full.
This is a scoped criterion comparison; it is not a whole tradition profile and it does not imply a respondent identity.
The single mapped criterion cannot establish utilitarianism, welfarism, or hedonism.

profiles.label: Ethical egoism — exclusive moral self-priority criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: One narrow normative criterion associated with ethical egoism: each agent's own long-term good is the ultimate moral end and another person's need alone supplies no independent moral reason. This does not represent the standard maximizing if-and-only-if account of moral rightness.
neighbors: Self-regarding prerogatives or duties of self-care
nonEntailments: That an act is morally right if and only if it best advances the agent's own good
That people in fact always act selfishly
That rationality always requires maximizing self-interest
Indifference to others or refusal to help
Rand's complete ethical system or any political position
unmeasuredAreas: The standard maximizing if-and-only-if criterion of moral rightness
Which theory of welfare or self-interest is correct
Rule-, character-, satisficing-, or other nonstandard variants of ethical egoism

claims.targetText: Each person morally ought to make their own long-term good the ultimate end of their actions; another person’s need alone supplies no independent moral reason.

sourceClaims.claim: The scholarly account distinguishes ethical egoism's moral focus on the agent's own good from psychological and rational egoism; its standard formulation is stronger than this scoped WVS criterion, so maximization remains explicitly unmeasured here.

nonEntailments: The standard claim that moral rightness is necessary and sufficient with maximizing the agent's own good
A descriptive claim that agents are always selfish
A claim that another person's interests never matter instrumentally
limitations: NE15 directly measures exclusive moral self-priority with a need-based discriminator, not the stronger maximizing criterion.
NEI100@1 and NEI101@1 share one authored evidence unit; Full obtains the second unit from NEI121@1 rather than treating the near-paraphrases as independent corroboration.
This is a one-criterion comparison and must not be presented as a complete ethical-egoism profile.
Only Full can assess the active proposition; Quick and Standard omission remains not measured.

profiles.label: Ayn Rand — life-grounded objective ethics criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: One selected commitment in Rand's ethics: requirements of human life and flourishing ground objective moral standards. This is not a reconstruction of Objectivism as a coordinated metaphysical, epistemological, ethical, and political system.
neighbors: Naturalistic or life-grounded ethics not derived from Rand
Ethical egoism without Rand's theory of value
nonEntailments: Objectivism as a complete philosophical system
Rand's specific rational-self-interest doctrine
Rand's theory of perception, concepts, or axiomatic knowledge
Rand's derivation of individual rights
Free-market or laissez-faire political commitments
unmeasuredAreas: Rand's rational self-interest within a life-grounded ethics
Rand's perceptual and conceptual epistemology
Rand's derivation and scope of individual rights
The wider metaphysical and political commitments of Objectivism

claims.targetText: Whether requirements of human life and flourishing ground objective moral standards. Separate from mere biological description or current preferences.

sourceClaims.locator: Passages on value and life as the standard, including the statement of man's life as the Objectivist standard of value (The Virtue of Selfishness, pp. 16–27)
sourceClaims.claim: Rand presents life as the standard of value and argues that objective ethics is grounded in the requirements of human life rather than in arbitrary preference.
The scholarly overview describes Rand's ethical theory as grounding value in the requirements of human life while situating that claim inside a larger system.

nonEntailments: Rational egoism or ethical egoism in every formulation
Rand's full epistemology or metaphysics
Rand's political theory or derivation of rights
limitations: ME09 captures only the life-and-flourishing grounding criterion.
The active NE15, EP20, and rights propositions are broader neighboring claims and remain insufficiently specific to fill Rand's other defining commitments.
This profile deliberately promotes one exact Rand-specific commitment, not Objectivism as a system.
Only Full can assess ME09; shorter-route omission must remain not measured.

profiles.label: John Stuart Mill — general happiness criterion (scoped)
profiles.scope: An internal, source-traceable comparison of John Stuart Mill's first-principle commitment to the general happiness as the ultimate moral standard; not a complete reconstruction of Mill's ethics, utilitarianism, or political philosophy.
nonEntailments: A settled classification of Mill as an act utilitarian
A settled classification of Mill as a rule utilitarian
A sanction-utilitarian reconstruction of duty
Adoption of the NE25 total-welfare promise-case commitment
Adoption of NE24 welfare-only outcome value
A simple quantitative hedonism
Mill's qualitative higher-pleasures doctrine
Mill's theory of liberty, rights, justice, or political economy
A complete Millian or utilitarian identity
unmeasuredAreas: Higher vs lower pleasures qualitative hierarchy
Harm principle and individual liberty boundaries
Representative democracy and epistemic voting
Secondary moral principles decision procedures
Act vs rule vs sanction utilitarian reconstruction
limitations: This comparison tests only the first-principle status of the general happiness standard.
It does not classify respondents as utilitarians or determine act vs rule consequentialism.
The proposition is evaluated only on the Full route; Quick and Standard routes leave it not measured.

claims.targetText: General happiness is the ultimate moral standard: moral rules, duties, and judgments are ultimately justified or resolved by their relation to the general happiness, without requiring that standard to be applied directly to each individual act.

sourceClaims.claim: Mill holds that the Greatest Happiness Principle is the foundation of morality, treating general happiness as the ultimate moral standard while recognizing secondary principles.
Scholars distinguish Mill's general happiness standard from decision procedures and record competing direct, rule, and sanction reconstructions.

nonEntailments: A settled classification of Mill as an act or rule consequentialist
An endorsement of total-welfare maximization in every dilemma
limitations: The claim is evaluated on the Full route only and does not establish a complete utilitarian worldview.
